match.reason: The closest bank points either frame sentence length around tone rather than pace (Year 8 card) or are pitched at Year 11 and cover fragments and inversion too, so none teaches this pace-focused idea at Stage 5 depth without a change of focus.

draft.title: Varying sentence length
card: Sentence length controls pace, which is how fast a reader moves through a text. Short sentences read quickly. Long sentences read more slowly.
A run of short sentences builds tension or speeds up action. Example: The door creaked. A shadow moved. Nobody breathed.

A long sentence can slow the reader down to take in detail or reflect. Example: Mia stood at the edge of the empty oval, remembering the summers she had spent there with friends who had since moved away.
Writers mix the two on purpose. A single short sentence after several long ones can stand out and hit hard.
draft.remember: Short sentences speed the pace up. Long sentences slow it down. Mixing them gives a writer control.

a.q: A writer describes a chase using these sentences: He ran. The gate slammed. Footsteps closed in. What effect do the short sentences mainly create?
opts: Slow pace and a thoughtful mood
Calm pace and a gentle mood
a.why: A run of short sentences moves the reader quickly, which suits a chase and builds tension. A thoughtful mood is the tempting wrong answer, because that effect comes from long sentences, not short ones.
a.clue: Think about how quickly short sentences are read.

b.q: Jess writes a story about a storm. After three long sentences describing the dark clouds and rising wind, she adds: The power died. Why is the final short sentence effective?
opts: It stands out after the long ones and hits hard
It slows the pace so the reader can reflect
It gives more detail about the storm clouds
It shows the writer is running out of ideas
b.why: After longer sentences, a single short one stands out and has a sudden, strong impact. Slowing the pace is the tempting wrong answer, because slowing the reader down is the job of long sentences.
b.clue: Look at how the short sentence differs from the ones before it.

b.best: It stands out after the long ones and hits hard
